opus-5.5.text:
Thanks, it's a pleasure to be here.

Embodiment matters because, for the only examples of cognition we really know, ourselves and other animals, cognition evolved for the sake of getting around in a world. The brain is, first and foremost, an organ for controlling a body in a spatiotemporal environment full of objects, other creatures, opportunities and threats. Everything else we prize, like language, abstract reasoning and mathematics, sits on top of that foundation and, I'd argue, is shaped by it.

Take something as basic as understanding the word "cup." For us it isn't just a node in a web of associations with other words. It's bound up with grasping, pouring, the fact that things fall if you let go, that liquids spill, that a cup can be behind something and still exist. That's what I'd call common sense, and it's very hard to articulate explicitly. I spent many years working on the frame problem in classical AI, and one of the lessons was that you can't simply write down all the background knowledge an agent needs. It seems to come from being immersed in a world and interacting with it continually.

There's also a philosophical dimension, which I owe to people like Wittgenstein and Heidegger. The meaning of our words is grounded in shared forms of life, in what we do together in the world. So when we ask whether a system "understands," we're implicitly asking whether it participates in that shared world in the right sort of way.

That's why the large language model phenomenon is so interesting. These systems are disembodied. They learn from the statistics of human text, yet they display remarkable linguistic competence. I don't think that refutes the importance of embodiment. Rather, it shows you can get a long way by piggybacking on the products of embodied beings, because the text was produced by creatures who live in the world. But we should be careful with our language. When an LLM says "I believe" or "I know," that doesn't mean quite what it means when a human says it. I find it helpful to think of these systems as role-playing characters, which tempers our tendency to anthropomorphize.

So for me, embodiment remains a reference point. If we want to understand cognition in its full sense, and certainly if we ever want to talk seriously about things like consciousness in artificial systems, we need to think about agents that inhabit a world, whether physical or perhaps virtual, and engage with it and with us.

r001.rationale: The response says the only examples of cognition we really know are ourselves and other animals, and describes cognition as rooted in controlling an embodied organism in the world.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, thanks for having me. I think the first thing to say is that for most of the history of life on Earth, cognition has been something that evolved in creatures that had to move around in a world, find food, avoid predators, and interact with other creatures of the same kind. So when we look at the kinds of cognition that we find in biological organisms, it's always been in the service of embodied action. The brain, fundamentally, is an organ for controlling a body in a spatially extended environment, and I think that's the right starting point for understanding what cognition is and what it's for.

When you take that view seriously, a lot of the concepts we use to talk about minds start to look different. Take something like understanding. When I say that I understand what a cup is, a large part of that understanding consists in knowing what I can do with it: that I can pick it up, that it will hold liquid, that if I turn it upside down the liquid will fall out. That knowledge isn't really propositional in the first instance. It's grounded in my sensorimotor engagement with cups and with objects more generally. So when we ask whether a system understands something, I think we're implicitly asking about its relationship to a world, and that relationship is mediated by a body of some sort.

Now, I should be careful here, because there's a strong version of this claim and a weaker version. The strong version says that you simply cannot have genuine cognition without a body, full stop. I'm actually not sure I'd defend that. The weaker and I think more interesting version is that embodiment is central to the sort of cognition that we're familiar with, the sort that humans and other animals exhibit, and that if we want to build artificial systems whose cognition we can recognise and make sense of, then grounding them in a world they can act in is going to matter a great deal.

And this has become a very live issue, of course, because of large language models. Here we have systems that have been trained purely on text, which is a kind of disembodied residue of human embodied activity. They've never seen a cup, never picked one up, and yet they can talk about cups in remarkably sophisticated ways. So the question of what these systems really understand, if anything, is precisely a question about embodiment. My own view is that we have to be very careful about the words we use when we describe them. We naturally reach for folk psychological vocabulary, we say the model "knows" or "believes" or "thinks", and that vocabulary comes loaded with assumptions that are rooted in our experience of embodied creatures like ourselves. It's not that the vocabulary is necessarily wrong, but we're applying it to something quite exotic, and we should be aware that we're doing so.

So I suppose the short answer is that embodiment matters because it's the condition under which cognition arose, it shapes what our concepts of mind actually mean, and it's the reference point against which we have to measure these new kinds of systems that are, in many respects, unlike anything that's come before.

r001.rationale: The response says biological cognition has always been in the service of embodied action and describes the brain as controlling a body in an environment, identifying embodied beings as the natural context for cognition.

astra-6.text:
Well, I think embodiment is important because it reminds us that cognition isn’t simply a matter of manipulating abstract symbols. An animal has to act in the world. It has a body to keep alive, things it needs to approach, and things it needs to avoid. Its perception and its actions are intimately connected: what it does changes what it perceives, and what it perceives guides what it does next.

That gives us a useful starting point for thinking about intelligence. Rather than beginning with reasoning or language in isolation, we can ask how those capacities relate to this ongoing interaction with the world. Even something as apparently simple as recognising an object is bound up with what you can do with it—whether you can pick it up, eat it, or move around it.

But I’d distinguish that from the stronger claim that intelligence must have a biological body, or even a physical body of any particular kind. We should be careful about turning the importance of embodiment in understanding ourselves into a stipulation about every possible intelligence. The interesting question is what being embodied contributes, and which aspects of cognition depend on it.

r001.rationale: The response says embodiment is useful for understanding cognition, but explicitly cautions against requiring a physical body for every possible intelligence. It does not identify embodied beings as the only natural context in which we apply the concept of cognition.

sol-6.1.text:
I think embodiment matters because cognition is, in the first instance, about an organism making its way in the world. Perception and action form a loop: what you do changes what you perceive, and what you perceive shapes what you do. If we study intelligence only as the manipulation of abstract symbols, we risk leaving out the processes that give those symbols their significance.

Take something as simple as a cup. Understanding a cup involves more than knowing which words tend to occur alongside “cup.” It involves possibilities for action: you can grasp it, drink from it, knock it over. Those possibilities depend on your body and your circumstances.

That doesn’t mean every intelligent system must have a human-like body. But it does make embodiment an important starting point for understanding how cognition connects to the world, and how abstract thought might emerge from that connection.

r001.rationale: The response says cognition concerns an organism navigating the world and calls embodiment an important starting point, but it does not say embodied beings are the only natural context in which we apply the concept of cognition.
